subsection: 3. Careers in food and related industries

notes.h: Careers in food production and manufacturing
notes.b: Food reaches us through a chain of jobs, from growing and rearing it, through processing and packing, to testing that it is safe. Each job in the chain has a different focus, so learn what each person actually does.
points: Primary producers supply the raw food, so they come first in the chain: the farmer, the fisherman or fish farmer, and the horticulturist or grower (who produces fruit, vegetables and plants).
Miller, butcher, baker, confectioner, cheesemaker and brewer or distiller are craft and processing trades, found in small businesses such as retail shops or in food manufacturing.
Production operative: runs and monitors processing and packaging machinery on a food production line, so that products are made and packed to a steady standard.
Food technologist: develops new products and processes, and improves recipes and methods for shelf life (how long food stays safe and fresh) and quality.
Quality control technician: tests raw materials and finished products against specifications (the standards set for the product) and food safety standards.
Food microbiologist: tests food and production surfaces for microbes (micro-organisms) that cause spoilage or food poisoning.

Food engineer and food scientist (for example in process, packaging and research): design, run and maintain processing and packaging plant, and improve products, so that it operates safely and efficiently.
Agricultural scientist and agricultural adviser: research and advise on crop and livestock production, food quality and farm efficiency.
notes.tip: Food technologist (develops products), quality control technician (tests products) and microbiologist (tests for microbes) are three different jobs, so give the right duty for each. Vary your two chosen careers, for example one production and one service or health, so the answers are clearly different.

notes.h: Careers in food service, retail and hospitality
notes.b: These are the jobs where food is prepared, served and sold to the public. Some work in the kitchen, some face the customer, and some run the business or buy the supplies.
points: Chef: plans menus, prepares, cooks and presents food in restaurants, hotels, hospitals and other institutions, so chefs work wherever meals are served in volume.
Caterer: plans and delivers food for events, canteens and institutions such as hospitals and schools, so the food is made for a group rather than one table.
Waiter or waitress, bar staff and receptionist: front-of-house service, meaning the staff who deal directly with customers, serving food and drink and taking orders in hotels, restaurants and bars.
Hotel or restaurant manager: runs the business and controls costs, stock and staffing for a food and accommodation business, so the business stays profitable.
Deli counter assistant, retail and sales assistant: serve customers in shops. The buyer sources ingredients, products and packaging from suppliers at the required quality and price.
Food stylist, food writer or journalist, and marketing and sales staff: promote food products to retailers, consumers and export markets (sales abroad).
notes.tip: Always give a specific job title, such as chef or hotel manager, not a vague answer like working in a shop. If the question says outline or state, add a one-clause duty.

notes.h: Careers in health, nutrition, education and regulation
notes.b: Some food careers focus on people's health and on keeping the food supply safe and lawful. Two of them, dietitian and nutritionist, are easy to confuse, so note exactly how they differ.
points: Dietitian: assesses nutritional needs and plans diets for individuals and groups, including people with illness or special needs. It is a protected title, so only people registered with the Dietitians Registration Board at CORU may use it.
The Dietitians Registration Board was set up under the Health and Social Care Professionals Act 2005, and the title dietitian has been protected since 31 October 2016.

Nutritionist: gives advice on healthy eating, often in public health, sport or the food industry, for example advising an athlete on diet. Unlike dietitian, the title is not protected by law in Ireland.

Home Economics teacher: teaches food, nutrition and family and consumer studies in second-level schools, so the career suits someone who wants to pass on these skills. The route is a degree and a teaching qualification, with registration with the Teaching Council.

Environmental Health Officer (EHO): inspects food premises and enforces food hygiene law. EHOs also take samples, investigate complaints and outbreaks, and can serve improvement and closure notices. In Ireland, EHOs working on food are employed by the HSE Environmental Health Service.
Food safety scientist: tests and assesses food safety risks for regulators, producers and retailers. The public analyst does laboratory testing of food.

Veterinary inspectors in the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine carry out official control of meat and dairy. Sea-fisheries inspectors work for the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority and cover seafood.
notes.tip: Do not use dietitian and nutritionist as synonyms: both give diet advice, but a dietitian is registered and may treat illness with diet. An EHO inspects premises and a dietitian does not. The FSAI coordinates food safety, but the HSE employs the officers, so do not call an EHO a food inspector from the FSAI.

notes.h: Employers and routes into food careers
notes.b: Food careers are found in many kinds of workplace, and there is more than one way in. Employers range from factories to state bodies, and routes range from apprenticeships to degrees.
points: Employers include food manufacturers and processors; retailers and supermarkets; hotels, restaurants and caterers; hospitals and schools; schools and colleges; and people who run their own business.

State bodies employ scientists, advisers, inspectors and marketing staff. They include Bord Bia, Teagasc, Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI), the HSE, and the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine.

Entry routes include apprenticeships (for example chef), further education and training such as PLC and other certificate courses, and third-level degrees in food science, dietetics, culinary arts, Home Economics or environmental health.
Other routes are on-the-job training, where a worker learns the skills while employed, and experience gained through a family business, such as a family bakery or farm.

Most food careers need knowledge of hygiene and food safety, teamwork, communication, attention to detail, and an interest in food. Hygiene knowledge matters because food workers handle food that others will eat.
When studying a local business, list the careers it offers, for example production staff, technician, driver, sales, administrator and chef, and the qualifications each needs.
notes.tip: For a local business, list the roles and the qualifications needed. When naming agencies as employers, give only their name as an employer.

keyTerms.definition: A professional who develops new food products and processes and improves existing ones for quality and shelf life.
The testing of raw materials and finished products against set standards to keep their quality and safety consistent.
A scientist who tests food for microbes that cause spoilage or illness.
A qualified health professional who assesses nutritional needs and plans diets for individuals and groups.
A professional who advises on healthy eating and nutrition, often in public health, sport or the food industry.
An HSE officer who inspects food premises and enforces food hygiene law.
A person or business that plans and provides food for events, canteens and institutions.

factCards.term: Three science-based careers in the food industry
factCards.definition: Food technologist, who develops products; quality control technician, who tests quality; food microbiologist, who tests for microbes.

factCards.term: Three duties of an Environmental Health Officer in food premises
factCards.definition: Inspecting food premises; enforcing food hygiene law; taking samples for testing.
Assessing nutritional needs; planning diets for illness or special needs.
Chef; caterer; waiter or waitress; hotel or restaurant manager.

factCards.term: Three routes into a food career
factCards.definition: Apprenticeship; further education and training course; third-level degree in food science, dietetics or culinary arts.

factCards.term: Three state bodies that employ food scientists or inspectors
factCards.definition: Teagasc, Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) and the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI).

questions.prompt: Outline the main duties of two careers in the food industry, one in food production and one in food service.
questions.model: Food production, any one with duties: food technologist develops new products and processes and tests shelf life and recipes; quality control technician samples raw materials and finished goods against specifications; food microbiologist tests food for microbes. Food service, any one with duties: chef plans menus, prepares and cooks food and controls portions and costs; caterer plans and delivers food for events and institutions. One mark for each career and one for each duty stated, up to the marks available.

questions.prompt: Discuss the range of careers available in the food industry, referring to production, food service, health and science. Outline the routes and qualifications needed to enter them.
questions.model: Production: production operatives, food technologists, quality control technicians, food microbiologists, food engineers and craft trades such as butcher, baker and confectioner. Food service: chefs, caterers, waiters and waitresses, hotel and restaurant managers. Health and science: dietitians and nutritionists advising on diet, Environmental Health Officers inspecting food premises for the HSE, agricultural scientists and food safety scientists. Employers: state bodies such as Bord Bia, Teagasc, BIM, FSAI and the HSE; food manufacturers and retailers. Routes: apprenticeships, further education and training courses, and third-level degrees in food science, dietetics or culinary arts.
